extra_snippets: Dutch privacy regulator AP this month advised consumers to not buy smart glasses, saying they are unsafe for both users and bystanders. In October, Dutch retail chain Hans Anders suspended sales of Meta's ​Ray-Ban smart glasses in the Netherlands and Belgium. Meta also faces proposed class-action lawsuits in the United States over alleged improper sharing of private images gathered by the glasses.

Dutch consumer groups, including Consumentenbond and Offlimits, have filed a lawsuit to halt Meta’s AI-powered smart glasses in the Netherlands over privacy and safety concerns, seeking a court injunction and hefty penalties.

AMSTERDAM, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Dutch consumer and digital rights groups asked a court on Thursday to halt sales of Meta AI-powered smart glasses in the Netherlands, arguing they violate European privacy laws by allowing wearers to film people without their knowledge. While limited in scope to the Netherlands, a summary ruling in the civil suit against Meta at the Amsterdam District Court could set a precedent amid growing public backlash, venue bans and regulatory warnings across the world.

The plaintiffs want Meta to prevent its glasses from being used to record people without their knowledge, stop using recordings to train AI models and halt sales until Meta complies. They sought penalties of €100,000 ($109,600) per day per defendant for non-compliance, capped at €100 million. Offlimits' lawyer Karlijn Han said the glasses were used for what she described in court as "creep shots."

results.title: First CJEU generative AI case: Advocate General considers AI training and press publishers' rights - Lexology
results.description: The First Advocate General Maciej Szpunar has recently delivered his Opinion in Like Company v Google Ireland Limited, the first generative artificial intelligence case to reach the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). The Opinion considers two distinct uses of press publications: (i) training large language models (LLMs) using protected material; and (ii) retrieving articles in real time through AI chatbots to answer users' queries.1 · On LLM training, the Advocate General recommends that the CJEU decline to rule because there was no evidence that Like Company's articles had been used to train Google's Gemini models.

extra_snippets: The First Advocate General Maciej Szpunar has recently delivered his Opinion in Like Company v Google Ireland Limited, the first generative artificial intelligence case to reach the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). The Opinion considers two distinct uses of press publications: (i) training large language models (LLMs) using protected material; and (ii) retrieving articles in real time through AI chatbots to answer users' queries.1 · On LLM training, the Advocate General recommends that the CJEU decline to rule because there was no evidence that Like Company's articles had been used to train Google's Gemini models.

That does not mean, however, that LLM training falls outside copyright law generally. For completeness, the Advocate General considers whether the copying involved in training can be permitted under the separate TDM exception in Article 4 of the CDSM Directive. His view is that LLM training ordinarily involves reproduction of protected material, including when material is scraped and copied to create a training dataset and processed during training, and that those reproductions may, as a rule, fall within the TDM exception because training involves automated analysis of digital text and data to extract patterns and relationships.

A similar approach to recognisable reproduction was taken by the Munich Regional Court in GEMA v OpenAI, where the court found infringement notwithstanding alterations to protected song lyrics reproduced in AI-generated outputs. The decision illustrates that identical reproduction is not necessarily required where protected elements remain recognisable.

results.title: EU Asset Managers Restrained from AI By Regulations - Law360
results.description: A trade body for European asset managers said in a report Wednesday that regulatory and compliance restrictions are among the significant barriers to adopting artificial intelligence and that policymakers should simplify the regulatory framework.
